name: Frames to timecode
seoTitle: Frames to timecode — Free Online Calculator
seoDesc: Frames to timecode: work out time in hours from the frames and the frame rate. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the frames and the frame rate and the Frames to timecode calculator solves for time in hours. It suits whatever you happen to be working on. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Frames to timecode calculator work?
sections.html:
The Frames to timecode calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports time in hours in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the frames and the frame rate.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Frames to timecode calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Time in hours=rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate)
Time in minutes=rounded down, (-60 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) + (1 ÷ 60) × frames ÷ frame rate)
Time in seconds=rounded down, (-3600 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) − 60 × rounded down, (-60 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) + (1 ÷ 60) × frames ÷ frame rate) + frames ÷ frame rate)
Excess frames=(-3600 × frame rate × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) − 60 × frame rate × rounded down, (-60 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) + (1 ÷ 60) × frames ÷ frame rate) − frame rate × rounded down, (-3600 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) − 60 × rounded down, (-60 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 3600) × frames ÷ frame rate) + (1 ÷ 60) × frames ÷ frame rate) + frames ÷ frame rate) + frames)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Frames to timecode calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the frames and the frame rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Frames to timecode calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — frames for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Frames to timecode calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns time in hours, derived from the frames and the frame rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Frames to timecode calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the frames and the frame rate, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Is the Frames to timecode calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
